purpose: Ipilimumab is used to treat certain types of cancer, most commonly melanoma (a serious type of skin cancer). It can also be used for kidney cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, and a few other cancers. It is sometimes used alone or combined with another immunotherapy drug called nivolumab.
how_it_works: Your immune system has natural 'brakes' that stop it from attacking your own body. Cancer cells can hijack these brakes to hide from your immune system. Ipilimumab blocks a protein called CTLA-4, which acts like one of those brakes, essentially releasing the brake so your immune system can find and attack the cancer cells more effectively.
common_side_effects: Tiredness and fatigue, diarrhea, rash or itchy skin, nausea, loss of appetite, stomach pain, and headache are among the most common side effects. Because this drug boosts your immune system, it can sometimes cause your immune system to attack healthy organs, which can be serious.
warnings: This is very important: because ipilimumab supercharges your immune system, it can cause serious inflammation in your lungs, colon, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, eyes, or skin. Call your doctor right away if you notice severe diarrhea, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, shortness of breath, vision changes, or unusual hormone symptoms like extreme fatigue or weight changes. These immune-related side effects can be life-threatening if not treated quickly. Always tell all your doctors you are on this medication.
typical_dosing: Ipilimumab is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) at a cancer clinic or hospital, typically over about 90 minutes. The most common dose is 3 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given once every 3 weeks for a total of 4 doses. Your doctor may adjust this schedule depending on your specific cancer and treatment plan.
